seoDescription: Learn how to create a Django project, initialize the starter files with django-admin startproject, open the project in an IDE (PyCharm suggested), and understand the core project structure including manage.py, the project package, settings.py, urls.py, and wsgi.py. Also learn how to run Django's built-in development server to preview your site locally and get best-practice pointers for where and when to edit files.

chapters.title: Creating the Django project with django-admin
chapters.description: Use django-admin startproject to create the starter files and directory for a new Django website.

chapters.title: Inspecting generated files and opening an IDE
chapters.description: Look inside the created directory to see generated files and open the project in an IDE (JetBrains/PyCharm recommended but optional).

chapters.title: Root directory vs inner project package and manage.py
chapters.description: Understand the difference between the outer root directory and the inner package with the same name, and learn what manage.py does and why you shouldn't edit it.

chapters.title: Project package files: __init__, settings, urls, and wsgi
chapters.description: Walk through the inner package files: __init__.py, settings.py, urls.py (URL routing overview), and wsgi.py (brief mention).

chapters.title: Running the built-in development server and next steps
chapters.description: Start Django's development server with manage.py runserver, open the local URL to see the default homepage, and plan the next tutorial steps.

summary:
## Key Concepts

- **django-admin startproject**: Creates the root directory and a core inner package containing the essential project files.

- **Project layout**: Outer directory name is arbitrary; the inner package (usually the same name) and its filenames are important.

- **manage.py**: A command-line utility for managing the project (migrations, runserver, createsuperuser, etc.). Do not edit this file.

- **__init__.py**: Marks the directory as a Python package; it can be empty.

- **settings.py**: Central configuration for the entire site (database, installed apps, middleware, templates, static settings). The tutorial defers detailed settings explanations until they become relevant.

- **urls.py**: URL declarations and routing — acts like a table of contents mapping URLs to views or behaviors (pages or actions like logout).

- **wsgi.py**: Web Server Gateway Interface entry point used for deploying to production; not needed for initial development work.

- **Development server (runserver)**: Django includes a lightweight local server for development. Use python manage.py runserver and open http://127.0.0.1:8000 to preview the site.

> [!TIP]
> Bookmark the local server URL (http://127.0.0.1:8000) to speed up testing.

> [!NOTE]
> You will edit settings.py, urls.py, and create app-level modules as development progresses; manage.py and wsgi.py are usually left untouched.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The outer project folder name is just a container—rename it freely. Keep the inner package and filenames generated by Django as they define project behavior.
transcription:
## Creating the Django project with django-admin

All right hostes. So now that we got Django downloaded and installed, set up properly on our computer, what we can do now is we can create our very first Django project.

So this is going to be the process that you go through anytime you want to create a new Django website, and that is this: go ahead and navigate to wherever you want to create your Django project files. I'm just going to stick mine on my desktop, why not, and type django-admin.

So this is a tool that we got whenever we downloaded Django and it allows us to do a bunch of cool things. In this video we're going to be using this to create the starter files, and these are just the core files that you have to include in every Django website. So the command for that is just startproject, so that's what that does.

Now the only other thing you need to type after this is you just need to give your project a name, and this is just the name of the directory. So usually this would be something like TheNewBoston if I was creating it for my website or like hockey website or something like that, but for this tutorial series I am just going to name it something super generic: website. So there you go. Hit enter and I'll show you guys what it did.

## Inspecting generated files and opening an IDE

So what that just did is it created this directory website, and if I double click this we can see that it made some files right in there. Now I am going to talk to you guys about what all these files are, but I'm actually going to open up an IDE and do it because I think it'll be a little bit better.

I'm actually using JetBrains—or excuse me—well yeah, JetBrains is the company that makes PyCharm, and this is the coolest IDE in the world. So if you guys want to use the same one then you can, but you don't need to. You can actually just follow along with this tutorial using Notepad or Sublime or anything you want and it's going to work fine.

But if you want to follow along with me then just go ahead and click Open and navigate to wherever you just made it. Mine was in my Desktop/website, so hit OK.

All right, mate, so that's a little bit better. I like having all my files on the left-hand side and then the content on the right so I can show you guys both things at once. But this is JetBrains. By the way, real quick, if you guys are using PyCharm then what you can do is if you go to File → New Project and click Django, then—you can just go ahead and give it a name and it just does the exact same thing as we just did. But if you don't, then go ahead and use the command line and boom, roasted, good to go.

## Root directory vs inner project package and manage.py

The first thing I want to mention is this root directory—this one that just got created—you can actually name that to whatever you want. The name doesn't really matter; it's just whatever you want to name it. It's just a container for all of the files inside. So it doesn't mean anything special to Django. However, the files inside here, their names are important.

We see that we have this directory right here which is the same name as its root directory, so that's why I said you can rename the parent one if it gets a little bit confusing, but keep this one the same.

Before we get to that, let's go ahead and talk about this file right here: manage.py. By the way, never edit this file. Never try to add anything to it; don't delete it. Just kind of ignore it. All this is, this manage.py, it's a program that comes with Django that lets you do a bunch of cool stuff to your project and it allows you to do things like access the database and create users for your website. We'll learn how to use this later on, but again this is not a file that we're ever going to want to touch or manage or edit or anything like that.

## Project package files: __init__, settings, urls, and wsgi

If you guys are like, all right, well where is the code that we're going to be working with? We're going to be working with some of the files in this directory and we're also going to be creating some other ones. Go ahead and expand this and I'll talk to you guys about all of these.

The first one, this __init__.py—all this is is a file that tells Python to view this directory as a Python package. Now there's actually nothing inside here, and that's because you don't even need any code in there. Again, like I said, it just says, 'Hey Python, this isn't just the normal directory on your computer; this is actually a Python package.'

Now the settings.py file: what I was going to do before this tutorial is I was like, all right, I'm going to go through all the settings and explain each one one by one, but then I was like, if I do that then people are probably just going to be like, all right, going to bed now, Django sucks, this is boring. So instead of just trying to explain all of these settings, what I'm going to do is I'm going to actually explain every single thing as we kind of need it and get to it. I think it'll be a lot better that way and it'll make a lot more sense than rather just trying to pound everything in your brain. But real quick, this file is just the settings and configuration options for your website—like the overall settings for your entire website. Just think of it like that.

Now this next one, urls.py: these are the URL declarations. In other words, it's kind of like the table of contents for your website, that's how people always explain it. What I mean by this is whenever you go to a website and you type in of course the website's name and then some URL after it, so whenever I type 'account' it gives me my stream; whenever I type 'forum' then it gives me the forum; whenever I type 'videos' or go to this URL then it shows me all the videos. So again, this part of the URL tells my website how to behave or what it's supposed to do.

Now most of the time you're going to give it a URL and it's going to return a web page, but sometimes it doesn't return a web page. Sometimes if you go to a URL like logout, then it actually just performs some functionality and logs the user out and doesn't just, you know, give you a web page. So again, what this file is is basically saying, 'Okay, look at whatever URL the user requested and then perform some functionality.' There's a lot more to it than that, but that's the basic overview of it; talk more about that later.

And this last one, wsgi.py—this stands for Web Server Gateway Interface—and it's just a special type of web server and we're going to learn about that a lot later. Don't even worry about it right now, but that's the basic overview of a core Django project.

## Running the built-in development server and next steps

So again, every single website that you have is going to be composed of all of these files. Again, you never touch this one and we're not going to be using this one a lot or this one, so it's actually a lot easier. Once we start getting into actually developing it you guys are going to see exactly what these do and it's going to make a lot more sense.

Yeah, that's the overview of it, and just to leave you guys with something cool: whenever you install Django and set it up like this it actually comes with a web server. It's not a full-featured web server like you would actually want to host an actual website with, but it comes with a little mini web server that you can use for development. So if you just want to boot it up and check out what our website looks like right now, then what you need to do is you need to navigate to wherever you created your project. I'm already in my desktop; I want to go ahead and navigate to website and just type ls and make sure that you see this, your project's name and manage.py, to make sure that you're in the correct location.

Again what we're going to be doing is we're going to be using this manage tool to boot our web server. Let me just go ahead and clear out of this to make it a little bit prettier. Now in order to do this type: python manage.py—and actually you don't even need that manage.py—this is a tool that we can use; it comes with a bunch of different features. What we're going to be doing is runserver. So again, we're just going to start that little development server that came with Django and it says: all right, so starting development server at http://127.0.0.1:8000. So if you just open up any web browser right now then you can go to this location and you should see this right there.

So again, Django came with a test server and right now we have a homepage looking beautiful. I actually bookmark this, that's why I have it right there, and that way I just don't have to type in the URL all the time, and that's what I recommend doing since you're going to be going to this page a lot. But anyways look at that—our very first Django website. In the next tutorial we're going to be spicing this up and it's going to be cool, so I'll see you then.
